programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Perthshire - Rebuilding an Ancient Settlement ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. After a devastating fire three years ago put the project in jeopardy, thatcher Scott is looking to the future and building a new cookhouse, using traditional techniques and local materials. It could mean big business for the centre and increased opportunities to work with the local community, but creating Iron Age dwellings in the modern age is anything but simple.
Will then heads off to Scone Palace, crowning place of Scottish kings, to meet a couple with a family heirloom in need of rescue. programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a place in the quarter-final. But two more high-pressure challenges, which will test every aspect of their cooking, stand in their way.
Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. In 2024, Adejoké became the first black woman in the UK to be awarded a coveted Michelin star. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.
It may sound simple, but this deceptively complex dish is packed with unfamiliar ingredients, techniques and flavours, and only one of the chefs has ever cooked moin moin before. With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. But with a place in the quarter-final on the line, get it wrong and the consequences could be huge.
Next up, it all comes down to dessert. The chefs have one last opportunity to convince Marcus and Monica that they deserve to stay in the competition.
But pastry is an unforgiving business. Every element must be precise, every second counts, and even the smallest mistake can unravel a dish. The judges want more than technical perfection… they’re looking for personality, originality, and a dessert that leaves a lasting impression. Who can hold their nerve when it matters most? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Highlands - Treasure in the Attic ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Joining Dom in the Highlands is Inverness-born traditional building conserver Rich. They are on the way to Nairn Museum, where renovations have revealed some unusual wall decorations – artworks painted directly on the bare walls of the museum's attic. Left behind by Polish soldiers stationed there during World War II, this art will be lost forever if it can’t be removed. However, removing century-old plaster is a delicate business, so there is no guarantee the artworks will survive the process.
Dom then travels to North Kessock to collect another precious item to be repaired back at the barn. He meets Carole, whose unusual clockwork ship in a glass dome evokes happy memories of childhood holidays in the Wester Ross village of Plockton. However, the paper sea it once sailed on is brittle and torn, and the tune no longer plays. Will David Burville be able to get this family heirloom - handed down from Carole’s great-aunt Elsie - making music on the high seas again?
While Dom and Rich have their hands full at the museum, Will is in Beauly to meet Alan MacPherson, who has gone from keen shinty player to shinty stick maker. Now producing more than 1,400 shinty sticks each year from his Highland workshop, Alan instructs Will in the intricacies of creating equipment to stand up to the rigors of this hard-fought game. Once the woodwork is over, it is time for Will to test his sporting prowess. programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
The four chefs who have survived the intensity of the heats are back in the kitchen. Now they must prove to Marcus and Monica that they have the consistency, confidence and creativity to take on the next level of the competition.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must put pistachio centre stage and show Marcus and Monica what they can do with it. It’s an ingredient that naturally lends itself to pastry and desserts, but used cleverly in a savoury dish, it could give one chef the edge. Will anyone dare to take it somewhere unexpected?
But the chefs aren’t finished yet. Their next test takes them out of the kitchen and into the company of three of the country’s most influential food critics: William Sitwell, Jimi Famurewa and, taking her place alongside them for the first time, Ixta Belfrage, a recipe developer and cookbook author who spent five years working at the Ottolenghi Test Kitchen.
The chefs must cook a two-course menu that showcases their food, ideas and technical ability, knowing that every element will be scrutinised by some of the toughest palates in the business. This is their chance to prove they can produce food that excites and surprises. However, impressing three professional critics is no easy feat, and their verdicts could have a major bearing on what happens next.
Back in the kitchen, Marcus and Monica must weigh up everything they have seen and tasted before deciding which chefs have done enough to progress. With only three places in knockout week available, one mistake, an underwhelming plate or a missed opportunity could make all the difference. Who will earn their place in the next stage – and whose journey ends here?
The pressure is mounting as the chefs edge closer to the coveted MasterChef: The Professionals title. Judge - Marcus Wareing Judge - Monica Galetti Series Editor - Antonia Lloyd Series Director - Emma Reynolds Executive Producer - Kelly Sparks Production Company - Shine TV.

Eric Knowles visits Nottingham’s Gothic revival cathedral to learn how conservators are revealing 19th-century artwork under decades of plaster and paint. programme.title: The Northumbria Mysteries
programme.desc:
When the body of a windsurfer washes ashore on Beadnell Bay, Rose and Joe are pulled into a murky case involving the intertwined worlds of funerals, windsurfing and dangerous spiked cigarettes.
The victim is identified as Andrew Bilton, stepson to Bev Bilton, a stern funeral director who quickly becomes suspect number one after Rose and Raj discover underlying resentments between her and her stepson. Complicating matters further, Bev is locked in an intense feud with Kass Moberly, a vibrant young funeral director who was secretly seeing Andrew before his death. As the investigation deepens, further tangled up in the case are Bev’s shifty deputy manager, Alfie, and Andrew’s tight-knit windsurfing crew, Noah and Chatri, who seem to be hiding secrets of their own.
Meanwhile, Joe launches his own off-the-books investigation into a local group of teenagers getting high at the priory, deeply concerned for their safety. What begins as a side project soon intersects directly with Rose’s murder case, revealing a shocking connection between the spiked cigarettes circulating among the youth and Andrew's unpleasant death.
Joining forces once again, Rose and Joe must navigate a muddle of illicit drug dealing, cut-throat commercial feuds, a shady ashes scandal and a volatile love triangle. Together, they traverse the Northumberland coast to piece together the truth and catch a killer before anyone else gets hurt, or worse... programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
International Men’s Day was established in 1999 to highlight positive male role models and raise awareness of men’s health and wellbeing. Ahead of this year’s event, Sean Fletcher is in Leeds exploring what it means to be a man in modern society, and how faith, friendship and a sense of purpose can help men thrive in mind, body and spirit.
He meets rugby league legend Jamie Jones-Buchanan, now CEO of Leeds Rhinos, where he made 421 appearances, as well as representing England and Great Britain. Jamie reflects on growing up without a father figure in one of the UK’s most deprived areas, and how rugby and his Christian faith provided positive male role models, and a sense of belonging and purpose. He challenges stereotypes of the macho rugby player, and his passion for helping the next generation comes to life during a training session.
In the Welsh valleys, Pastor John Funnell reflects on the extraordinary number of young men joining his congregation. John left a highly paid career after becoming a Christian and moved to one of Europe’s most deprived communities. He explains how his church offers practical skills, mentoring, friendship and faith, helping men see that their past does not have to determine their future.
Back in Leeds, Sean meets Chris Sayburn, a minister and renowned worship leader who spent 12 years living with chronic pain following complications after spinal surgery. He tells Sean how exercise and faith have helped him rebuild his life and how a community of men became a lifeline.
With uplifting hymns and songs from around the UK.
1. Sweet Heart of Jesus - Leeds Cathedral 2. Amazing Grace - The Kingdom Choir 3. Facing a Task Unfinished - Lisburn Cathedral 4. Lord of All Hopefulness - Chris Sayburn and Friends 5. programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The open ocean is the largest wilderness on earth. Covering more than half of the planet's surface, it appears at first glance to be an endless blue desert. Yet hidden here are some of the most extraordinary animals.
We uncover the surprising strategies, epic journeys and remarkable resilience that allows life to thrive here. From wandering predators and drifting castaways to giant whales and tiny turtle hatchlings, it is a world where life survives against the odds.
The journey begins far beyond the sight of land, where California sea lions travel miles into the Pacific in search of seasonal, rich fishing grounds. Here, they join one of the open ocean's great feeding spectacles as black skipjack tuna, mahi-mahi and seabirds converge on vast schools of fish in a dramatic battle for a meal.
Some animals aren’t just visitors here; they spend their entire lives in this immense expanse. Rough-toothed dolphins have roamed the oceans since before woolly mammoths walked the earth, and yet we know very little about them. To help find food, they use sophisticated teamwork and ingenious hunting techniques that have rarely been witnessed.
Although the open ocean seems like a featureless expanse, it is shaped by powerful currents that flow across the globe like invisible rivers. These currents transport animals, nutrients and entire ecosystems across immense distances. For ocean drifters such as Smith's swimming crabs, the currents are both a lifeline and a gamble, carrying them through a world where danger can appear without warning.
Currents also drive one of the largest floating ecosystems on the planet. Today, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt stretches over 5,000 miles across the ocean. But changing conditions are sweeping unprecedented amounts of this seaweed onto coastlines throughout the Caribbean. On the beaches of Mexico, turtle hatchlings emerging from their nests face a daunting new obstacle as mountains of sargassum block their path to the sea. Their struggle reveals how changes in the open ocean can have profound consequences far beyond the horizon.
In the Pacific, we follow one of nature's greatest aerial pirates, a frigatebird mother raising her chick alone.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. After a devastating fire three years ago put the project in jeopardy, thatcher Scott is looking to the future and building a new cookhouse, using traditional techniques and local materials. It could mean big business for the centre and increased opportunities to work with the local community, but creating Iron Age dwellings in the modern age is anything but simple.
Will then heads off to Scone Palace, crowning place of Scottish kings, to meet a couple with a family heirloom in need of rescue. It’s a handwritten Gaelic piping music book, handed down from Ian’s great-grandfather Donald, known as the Hero of Alma after his actions in the Crimean War. Now severely damaged, the music in its brittle pages might be lost forever if bookbinder Chris Shaw cannot bring it back from the brink. Ian will never play the songs it contains, as he has been battling motor neurone disease for the past decade, but he hopes if Chris Shaw is successful, the book can be passed down to his own son, also named Donald in honour of his ancestor.
Always in search of a new challenge, Dom joins a Perth-based family business whose handmade sporrans are the perfect accessory to Scotland’s famous kilts. It’s a critically endangered heritage craft that dates back to the 12th century, and the family is turning to technology to keep up with the challenge faced by cheaper, mass-produced versions made abroad. Dom is always eager to get on the tools, so what will his hosts make of his attempts at leatherworking? programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: The Northumbria Mysteries
programme.desc:
When the body of a windsurfer washes ashore on Beadnell Bay, Rose and Joe are pulled into a murky case involving the intertwined worlds of funerals, windsurfing and dangerous spiked cigarettes.
The victim is identified as Andrew Bilton, stepson to Bev Bilton, a stern funeral director who quickly becomes suspect number one after Rose and Raj discover underlying resentments between her and her stepson. Complicating matters further, Bev is locked in an intense feud with Kass Moberly, a vibrant young funeral director who was secretly seeing Andrew before his death. As the investigation deepens, further tangled up in the case are Bev’s shifty deputy manager, Alfie, and Andrew’s tight-knit windsurfing crew, Noah and Chatri, who seem to be hiding secrets of their own.
Meanwhile, Joe launches his own off-the-books investigation into a local group of teenagers getting high at the priory, deeply concerned for their safety. programme.desc:
Nadiya presents the very best weekend breakfasts for kicking back, relaxing and really indulging in the pleasure of the day’s first meal. And, of course, they are all easy, effortless and baked in the oven.
First up are Nadiya’s delectable granola cupcakes for a delicious breakfast on the go. A sticky fruit-and-nut granola shell is filled with chocolate and yoghurt before being crowned with edible flowers and fruit.

And, for a little indulgence at the weekend, this vibrant fruity delight is topped with crispy coconut croissant bites, a flurry of crushed frozen raspberries and a drizzle of yoghurt and honey.
Nadiya’s sweet breakfast wraps have a deliciously gooey baked banana and peanut butter filling, encased in a sugary, spiced tortilla wrap and drizzled with decadent dark chocolate. They are a perfectly indulgent way to relax into the weekend, as a batch can be baked in a matter of minutes.
Finally, Nadiya shares one of her best-ever rule-breaking recipes. She takes the traditional English fry-up to a new level by turning it into a pizza topping. Pillowy soft pizza dough with a crisp crust, smothered in a tomato and baked bean base and topped with succulent sausage, moreish mushrooms, tangy cheese, crispy onions and a perfectly runny egg. This might not be one for the purists, but it is the breakfast of champions.
Meanwhile, 18-year-old baker Kitty Tait from Oxfordshire shares her ingenious recipe for za’atar honey and feta swirls. At just 14, Kitty started to suffer from debilitating anxiety, but with the help of her dad, discovered that the simple pleasure of baking bread transformed her mental health. Kitty’s love of baking blossomed, and she now runs an acclaimed artisan bakery and is definitely a star of the future. programme.title: BBC Children in Need
programme.sub-title: Sian Eleri’s BBC Children in Need Road Trip ║ 2026
programme.desc:
Radio 1 presenter Sian Eleri takes on an almighty challenge when BBC Children in Need’s Pudsey Bear sends her on a Wales-wide road trip. Her mission is to find six Children in Need-funded projects across Wales that support the development and well-being of young people. But Pudsey doesn’t make it easy. Each step of the way, she must solve one of Pudsey’s riddles before she can proceed to her next destination. The bear has also roped in BBC 1’s Morning Live presenter Gethin Jones and Radio 2’s early breakfast show host Owain Wyn Evans to bamboozle Sian on her journey.
The first project is at Tal Y Sarn farm on Anglesey, where BBC Children in Need-funded gymnastics sessions helped 18-year-old Abby overcome anxiety and an eating disorder. Next, Sian visits Theatr Clwyd in Mold. There, she meets Eleanor, who has global developmental delay and autism. Sian hears how the Theatr’s Fuse sessions give Eleanor an important creative outlet and safe space to make friends and build her confidence.
Sian’s third project is ASD Rainbows in Mountain Ash in the Cynon Valley. Here, BBC Children in Need funding pays for staffing for an after-school club which supports neurodivergent children like seven-year-old Olly. And in Cardiff Bay, Sian learns how a grant to the project Silkfutures, to support rap music sessions, has helped develop many young people’s self-confidence and given them the space to express themselves freely.
Next is Talking Hands, a charity in Swansea that teaches British Sign Language and supports deaf youngsters in Wales like eight-year-old Tom. Sian’s final project is Surfability. Based at Caswell Bay beach on the Gower peninsula, it helps children with additional needs and their siblings go surfing together. Here, the Radio 1 presenter has the chance to meet twin brothers Jakey and Ethan and see how Jakey, who has Down’s syndrome and is non-verbal, takes to the surfboard like a duck to water.
Along the way, Sian’s resilience is tested when she takes up pottery, mountain biking, surfing and open-air swimming before being reunited with Pudsey, who surprises her with an end-of-road trip wrap party.

Meanwhile, social worker Nicola has news for Sinead when she drops in for a surprise inspection and tells her that Beacon Fold is going into special measures. Sinead, always a fan of a challenge, says she can do it in three months, an offer that Nicola happily accepts. programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo crosses the Culloden Viaduct aboard the Caledonian Sleeper to arrive bright and early in the coastal city of Inverness, from where he heads north on a magnificent scenic adventure to the Orkney archipelago.
On boggy moorland overlooking the Moray Firth near Inverness, Michael explores the battlefield at Culloden, where Bonnie Prince Charlie’s Jacobite army fought British government troops in 1746. Today, ponies and cattle help to preserve the character of the landscape as it was 275 years ago. Michael learns to execute the infamous Highland Charge and discovers how the Jacobites’ catastrophic defeat devastated the Highlands for years to come.
Excellent sea and rail links and swathes of lush pine forest in this coastal region have given rise to a strong timber industry. Michael investigates the production of oriented strand board for the construction industry at an Inverness mill, which manufactures 16 million boards annually.
The Highland mainline climbs the Slochd summit to deliver Michael to the village of Carrbridge, home of the World Porridge Making Championships. At stake is a golden spurtle – does Michael’s whisky-flavoured mushroom porridge risotto stand a chance?
At Broomhill, Michael’s dreams come true when he is invited to join the crew of the Strathspey Steam Railway on the footplate of their wonderful locomotive as they puff and pant their way past the River Spey and the Cairngorm mountains along the original main line from Inverness to Perth.
At Aviemore, Michael heads into Cairngorms National Park to admire its epic scenery. On the banks of Loch Morlich, he learns about writer, poet and naturalist Nan Shepherd, who captured the essence of the Cairngorms in her prose. Presenter - Michael Portillo Director - Beatrice Ni Bhroin Series Editor - Alison Kreps Executive Producer - John Comerford Production Company - Fremantle.

programme.title: Rise of the Rockstar Chef
programme.desc:
Every chef dreams of a Michelin star. Episode two of Rise of the Rockstar Chef follows the hunt for that recognition, and for the leap that separates the great from the legendary. Moving from one star to two is hard, but the hardest jump of all is from two to three.
Marco Pierre White made that leap, becoming the first British chef to win three Michelin stars, and the youngest ever to do so. The episode explores what the pursuit demanded and what it cost. Marco reflects on the price of perfection. and how success also brings a rupture. Gordon Ramsay, who learned his craft under Marco, leaves to build his own name, and both men look back on the emotion of that parting. When menus from Aubergine begin appearing on Marco's desk, the friendship is over.
Gordon recounts the story of the stealing of the restaurant’s reservation book, the crown jewels of any restaurant, revealing just how bitter the split became. Marcus Wareing, Gordon's first employee, recalls the early days of Gordon's kitchen and the fierce ambition driving it.
As the 90s unfold, Heston Blumenthal’s drive, creativity and uncompromising pursuit of excellence transforms modern British cuisine. Heston cooks in a completely different way, and his food blows minds. It is pure theatre, with equipment unlike anything seen in a normal kitchen. Dishes such as the triple-cooked chip, taking two years to perfect, went on to change not just food but kitchens in restaurants and at home. With the opening of The Fat Duck, his home is on the line, and the need for success is huge.
Meanwhile, the empires expand. Marco and Gordon take over the kitchens of some of London's top hotels, and their restaurants become the places to be. Marco’s restaurant Titanic draws the Spice Girls, Oasis, footballers and the tabloids, with as many as 4,000 guests passing through in a single night - a 90s Studio 54. Contributors describe the energy of those years, and the revolutionary push for creativity in ways never seen before. When Heston is crowned the number one chef in the world, he voices the immensity of the pressure, his inferiority complex and the highs and lows of extreme success. Presenter - Ellie Taylor Executive Producer - Rhe-an Archibald Series Editor - Richard Berkshire Series Producer - Ross Proudfoot.

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Beginning today on the Moray Firth, Michael admires the impressive Cullen viaduct before enjoying a bowl of Cullen skink at a family-run fishmonger of 150 years’ standing. In the factory smokery, he learns from the owner how the famous soup acquires its distinctive taste.
Heading west along the firth, Michael reaches Forres Station and the seaside village of Findhorn, where he meets members of an eco-community founded in the 1960s. At the Findhorn Foundation, Michael discovers spiritual energy, sacred dancing and a history of very large vegetables.
Michael’s next destination is Ardersier and the mighty Fort George, which sits on an isolated spit of land jutting west into the firth. Its huge boundary walls and heavy guns at every approach are an awe-inspiring sight. Michael hears why it was built on this coast in the mid-18th century and the role it has played in Britain’s strategic defence, which continues to the present. He meets members of the Black Watch, part of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, who are based at the fort today. He also listens to a pipe and drum rehearsal and is permitted by Scotty the tailor to try on the regimental sergeant major’s jacket.
Nestled in woods next to the River Nairn, Michael discovers a romantic Scottish tower house, Cawdor Castle. Guided by Lady Cawdor, Michael discovers the castle’s literary connections to a tragic Scottish hero. On the castle lawn, around the cauldron, Michael joins the witches to hail Macbeth, Thane of Cawdor. The brand new £8m boat was part-financed by a huge bank loan and built to withstand the toughest conditions off Scotland’s west coast. When the squid prove elusive, the pressure starts to mount. But could the arrival of a winter storm see Endeavour’s rivals forced back to harbour, giving it a monopoly over the squid grounds? programme.title: Rise of the Rockstar Chef
programme.desc:
Every chef dreams of a Michelin star. Episode two of Rise of the Rockstar Chef follows the hunt for that recognition, and for the leap that separates the great from the legendary. Moving from one star to two is hard, but the hardest jump of all is from two to three.
Marco Pierre White made that leap, becoming the first British chef to win three Michelin stars, and the youngest ever to do so. The episode explores what the pursuit demanded and what it cost. Marco reflects on the price of perfection. and how success also brings a rupture. Gordon Ramsay, who learned his craft under Marco, leaves to build his own name, and both men look back on the emotion of that parting. When menus from Aubergine begin appearing on Marco's desk, the friendship is over.
Gordon recounts the story of the stealing of the restaurant’s reservation book, the crown jewels of any restaurant, revealing just how bitter the split became. Marcus Wareing, Gordon's first employee, recalls the early days of Gordon's kitchen and the fierce ambition driving it.
As the 90s unfold, Heston Blumenthal’s drive, creativity and uncompromising pursuit of excellence transforms modern British cuisine. Heston cooks in a completely different way, and his food blows minds. It is pure theatre, with equipment unlike anything seen in a normal kitchen. Dishes such as the triple-cooked chip, taking two years to perfect, went on to change not just food but kitchens in restaurants and at home. With the opening of The Fat Duck, his home is on the line, and the need for success is huge.
Meanwhile, the empires expand. Marco and Gordon take over the kitchens of some of London's top hotels, and their restaurants become the places to be. Marco’s restaurant Titanic draws the Spice Girls, Oasis, footballers and the tabloids, with as many as 4,000 guests passing through in a single night - a 90s Studio 54. Contributors describe the energy of those years, and the revolutionary push for creativity in ways never seen before. When Heston is crowned the number one chef in the world, he voices the immensity of the pressure, his inferiority complex and the highs and lows of extreme success. Presenter - Ellie Taylor Executive Producer - Rhe-an Archibald Series Editor - Richard Berkshire Series Producer - Ross Proudfoot.

For some of the chefs, the ingredients and techniques are entirely unfamiliar, and with no recipe to follow, they’ll need to draw on their experience, trust their seasoned palates and remain composed under pressure. With a place in the quarter-final at stake, can they rise to Alex’s exacting challenge, or will this intricate test prove a step too far?

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo’s Scottish coastal railway journey reaches Invergordon on the Cromarty Firth, the third great inlet on the northeast coast of the Highlands. He arrives on Britain’s northernmost railway, the Far North Line, and heads straight onto the water to explore a former oil drilling rig now moored in the firth. It’s easier said than done; Michael is hoisted into the air by crane as he clings to a 'personnel basket'. The decline of the oil industry since its peak in the 1990s means that rather than drilling wells, this rig now caps old ones, securing them with cement. Michael helps to assemble a pipe that could stretch up to two miles long.
Michael’s next stop is Fearn, from which he heads to the mudflats and saltmarsh of Nigg Bay and its Global Energy Park. Michael hears how both the area and personnel have moved away from oil and gas to renewables and marvels at the colossal scale of the wind turbines he sees being readied for transport offshore. He discovers the blades for one tower are longer than a standard football pitch!
On the shore of the Dornoch Firth, Michael helps to reintroduce his favourite delicacy to the firth’s shallow waters. Oysters were plentiful in this region for thousands of years, but their great popularity during the 19th century led to a catastrophic decline. Now oysters are beginning to flourish again, and Michael joins Herriot Watt University’s team effort to establish 200,000 oysters at Dornoch within the next three years.
Michael’s next stop is the Glenmorangie Whisky Distillery, also located on the banks of the Dornoch Firth. The science and art of whisky production are revealed to Michael as he tours the distillery. Presenter - Michael Portillo Director - Beatrice Ni Bhroin Series Editor - Alison Kreps Executive Producer - John Comerford Production Company - Fremantle.

programme.title: The Future with Hannah Fry
programme.desc:
Pain is a fact of life. For many, it is excruciating and inescapable, a truly disruptive force. But amid the continuing fallout of the global opioid crisis, new technologies are being developed every day to limit and potentially even eliminate pain.
Professor Hannah Fry learns about the future of pain management and how revolutionary technologies are being developed to directly control pain signals. programme.title: The Repair Shop
programme.desc:
First into the barn is Gary from Hastings, bringing his father Jimmy’s old butcher’s bike. Built for heavy loads, it was used to carry boxes of meat through Hastings in the 1950s before becoming part of Jimmy’s wider life on the seafront, where he worked as a fisherman and later as a 'boy ashore', helping boats land their catch. Tragedy struck in the infamous storm of 1987, when Jimmy perished while trying to save fishing boats from the violent seas. Soon after, his friends created the Crown Lane bike race in his honour, with Jimmy’s old delivery bike at the centre of the event. For nearly four decades, thousands of competitors have pedalled the heavy machine uphill for charity, but years of wear have left it unsafe to ride. Bike restorer Tim Gunn sets about strengthening its frame, fixing brakes and cranks, and ensuring it is safe for the future, while Dom Chinea adds a new hand-painted advertising board to honour Jimmy’s memory.
Next, father and son Paddy and Gary travel from Belfast with a prized pair of motorcycle racing goggles belonging to Paddy’s father, George Brockerton. George was an extraordinary competitor who began his motorbike journey as a teenage dispatch rider in the First World War before becoming a celebrated racer. He competed in the Ulster Grand Prix, the Isle of Man TT, and in 1935 became the only known Irishman to win a coveted Brooklands Gold Star after breaking the 100mph barrier – a feat almost unheard of at the time. His goggles, once a symbol of daring speed and personal pride, have deteriorated, their brittle latex eyepieces crumbling with age. Shoemaker Dean Westmoreland and plastics expert Charlotte Abbott join forces to carefully recreate the missing parts, preserving the distinctive shape and colour so that Paddy and Gary can once again celebrate George’s achievements.
From Mid Wales, Amanda arrives with a mysterious painting known as The Last Gathering, found in the attic of her family’s farmhouse near Mynydd Epynt. The artwork captures a rural ritual, where farmers would bring livestock down from the mountains for shearing and selling - a practice that ended abruptly when the community was evicted during the Second World War to make way for a Ministry of Defence training ground.

programme.title: Murder Case
programme.desc:
On New Year's Eve 2016, 23-year-old university student Cameron Logan and his girlfriend, 24-year-old journalist Bex Williams, are celebrating the new year. After partying into the small hours at a friend’s house, they walk home together to Cameron’s family home in an affluent suburb of Glasgow, where they were staying overnight. In the early morning of 1 January, Bex and Cameron wake in terror with their bed on fire, and, within seconds, flames have engulfed the entire room.
Telling her story fully for the first time, Bex Williams recalls the horror of those initial moments. Crawling through the smoke and flames in search of a way out, she tries to escape through the kitchen but discovers the back door is locked. In a remarkable act of ingenuity, she opens the freezer and puts her head in, just before losing consciousness. Cameron’s parents are woken by the chaos and manage to escape with minor injuries, and Bex is pulled to safety and rushed to hospital. Cameron’s older brother Blair returns home to find his family home overcome by fire, with firefighters and police already at the scene.
This is just the beginning of the horror story for Bex and the Logan family, as Cameron has not made it out alive. Once the fire is brought under control, detectives and forensic experts begin to examine the scene. What initially appears to be a devastating house fire soon takes a sinister turn. Inside the property, investigators discover the unmistakable smell of petrol, and Cameron’s mother says she saw a masked figure throw something into the living room where Cameron and Bex were sleeping, before fleeing the property.
Police Scotland’s Major Investigation Team is now faced with a murder investigation and a baffling question: why would anyone target this family? With the clock ticking, the team begin to meticulously piece together the evidence from the scene and build a picture of the events of that night. With no obvious motive to investigate, detectives must follow every lead as they try to understand what really happened inside this family home.
Meanwhile, Bex is in intensive care fighting for her life and is put in a medically induced coma. As soon as she wakes, detectives are keen to speak to her.

programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
Michael Portillo's coastal railway journey takes him past lochs and castles on the Far North Line to Britain’s northernmost railway station at Thurso. From Lairg on the banks of Loch Shin, Michael heads for a secret conservation area in the 18-mile-long loch to track down one of Scotland’s most elusive and endangered species, the freshwater pearl mussel. Michael wades into the water with an expert on the mollusc, who shows him how to spot their shells underwater through a glass-bottomed cone and explains why they are so highly prized.
A glorious journey along the valley of the River Fleet delivers Michael to Dunrobin Castle station, which serves the castle, seat of the earls and dukes of Sutherland since the 13th century. Michael finds out about the second duke of Sutherland, who planned in the mid-19th century to clear his land of crofters in order to graze sheep. His name is forever associated with the misery and destruction of the Highland Clearances.
At Brora, Michael hears how the Clearances affected the crofters evicted by the duke and learns about the purpose-built fishing villages to which they were sent. Two modern-day crofters show Michael how they are turning part of their coastal croft into a low-intensity farm.
Back on the Far North Line, built by the third duke of Sutherland, Michael reaches Georgemas Junction, Caithness, where the local stone is a much-sought-after construction material. At Spittal Mains quarry, Michael learns to split a flagstone by hand with a heavy hammer. Presenter - Michael Portillo Director - Beatrice Ni Bhroin Series Editor - Alison Kreps Executive Producer - John Comerford Production Company - Fremantle.

The chefs must find the perfect balance, using their creativity and instinct to showcase saffron at its best. programme.title: Great Coastal Railway Journeys
programme.desc:
From Britain’s northernmost station at Thurso in Caithness, Michael Portillo heads for the ferry port of Scrabster to cross the Pentland Firth to the Orkney Islands. Passing the Old Man of Hoy, Michael takes in stunning views of the Orkney archipelago and the rugged coastlines of its 70 islands.
Michael reaches land at Stromness on the largest of the islands, Mainland, and heads for Kirkwall, its most historic town. A visit to St Magnus Cathedral with a Norwegian historian sheds light on how much history the Orkneys share with Norway.
Back in Stromness harbour, Michael joins a diving expedition to the former British naval base at Scapa Flow. It’s one of the largest sheltered natural harbours in the world, well-placed for both the North Sea and the Atlantic. As divers explore the wreck of a dreadnought battleship, Michael hears how, in the aftermath of the First World War, nearly the entire German navy was scuttled here.
Michael discovers defensive measures taken during the Second World War in massive causeways designed to seal the harbour’s eastern entrances and learns about the beautiful, surprising legacy of the Italian prisoners of war who constructed them.
From Mainland, Michael flies to North Ronaldsay, which lies further north than the southern tip of Norway and is known for its rare breed of coastal sheep. The youngest councillor on the Orkney Islands introduces Michael to her fellow islanders and their native, seaweed-eating sheep. Michael helps to patch up the 200-year-old sheep dyke, a Grade A listed drystone wall around 12 miles long.
Back on Mainland, Michael admires the towering sea stack, Yesnaby Castle, located on the spectacular coastline, which inspired one of Britain’s greatest 20th-century composers and conductors, Sir Peter Maxwell Davies. Michael learns about his prolific career from his partner, and on the cliffs at Yesnaby, listens to a string arrangement of his best-known work, Farewell to Stromness, played by schoolchildren from the island. Presenter - Michael Portillo Director - Beatrice Ni Bhroin Series Editor - Alison Kreps Executive Producer - John Comerford Production Company - Fremantle.

programme.title: Trawlermen: Hunting the Catch
programme.desc:
Three hundred thousand square miles of ocean. Three GPS-tracked voyages, filmed around the clock. One week at sea.
Emilia Jayne hunts for cuttlefish in the world’s busiest shipping lane. Cargo ships have right of way here, but lucrative cuttlefish swim in these grounds too. After finding good fishing at the start of his week-long trip, can skipper Luke Selvey keep the secret to himself?
Margaret of Ladram is Brixham’s most successful trawler. This week, skipper Adam Cowan Dickie is gambling – he’s leaving his home waters of the English Channel behind and steaming 20 hours to the Bristol Channel. His target is Dover sole, one of the most expensive fish in British waters. Struggling to cover his expenses, Adam ups the stakes and targets an ancient ship wreck and the notoriously soft ground of the ‘gravel pits’.
Westro skipper Stephen West is the youngest skipper in Scotland’s prawn fleet. This week, he goes it alone and fishes far away from the rest of the fleet, heading into storm force winds. As the early hauls of the net end in failure, Stephen has a decision to make: continue to tow for prawns or cut and run to the rest of the fleet further north and join forces with his brother Andrew on Forever Faithful. programme.title: Flog It
programme.desc:
This episode comes from the Fleet Air Arm Museum situated on HMS Heron, the naval aviation base in Yeovilton, Somerset. Paul Martin is joined by experts Charlie Ross and Thomas Plant, and together they pick out a selection of interesting antiques to be sold at a local auction.
Paul finds out about one of Europe's largest helicopter squadrons which operates out of HMS heron and takes to the skies. He also goes behind the scenes at the museum, where he meets curator Dave Morris, whose pioneering way of working is bringing exhibits to life in a way never previously imagined. programme.title: Panorama
programme.desc:
Warren Arter was seen as a star detective in the Metropolitan Police, but he was also a sexual predator. He used his position running a rape and sexual offences unit to groom and sexually exploit vulnerable women whose cases he investigated. But the Met missed a string of opportunities to stop Arter and then suspended him on full pay for almost seven years before finally dismissing him for drug offences in 2023.
In 2024, he was with his wife Rebekah when she died in a hotel room in Barbados in mysterious circumstances. Reporter Noel Titheradge investigates the case that has been called the Met's 'dirty secret' and tracks down new witnesses who tell him what really happened. programme.title: Songs of Praise
programme.desc:
International Men’s Day was established in 1999 to highlight positive male role models and raise awareness of men’s health and wellbeing. Ahead of this year’s event, Sean Fletcher is in Leeds exploring what it means to be a man in modern society, and how faith, friendship and a sense of purpose can help men thrive in mind, body and spirit.
He meets rugby league legend Jamie Jones-Buchanan, now CEO of Leeds Rhinos, where he made 421 appearances, as well as representing England and Great Britain. Jamie reflects on growing up without a father figure in one of the UK’s most deprived areas, and how rugby and his Christian faith provided positive male role models, and a sense of belonging and purpose. He challenges stereotypes of the macho rugby player, and his passion for helping the next generation comes to life during a training session.
In the Welsh valleys, Pastor John Funnell reflects on the extraordinary number of young men joining his congregation. John left a highly paid career after becoming a Christian and moved to one of Europe’s most deprived communities. He explains how his church offers practical skills, mentoring, friendship and faith, helping men see that their past does not have to determine their future.
Back in Leeds, Sean meets Chris Sayburn, a minister and renowned worship leader who spent 12 years living with chronic pain following complications after spinal surgery. He tells Sean how exercise and faith have helped him rebuild his life and how a community of men became a lifeline.
With uplifting hymns and songs from around the UK.
1. Sweet Heart of Jesus - Leeds Cathedral 2. Amazing Grace - The Kingdom Choir 3. Facing a Task Unfinished - Lisburn Cathedral 4. Lord of All Hopefulness - Chris Sayburn and Friends 5. programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The open ocean is the largest wilderness on earth. Covering more than half of the planet's surface, it appears at first glance to be an endless blue desert. Yet hidden here are some of the most extraordinary animals.
We uncover the surprising strategies, epic journeys and remarkable resilience that allows life to thrive here. From wandering predators and drifting castaways to giant whales and tiny turtle hatchlings, it is a world where life survives against the odds.
The journey begins far beyond the sight of land, where California sea lions travel miles into the Pacific in search of seasonal, rich fishing grounds. Here, they join one of the open ocean's great feeding spectacles as black skipjack tuna, mahi-mahi and seabirds converge on vast schools of fish in a dramatic battle for a meal.
Some animals aren’t just visitors here; they spend their entire lives in this immense expanse. Rough-toothed dolphins have roamed the oceans since before woolly mammoths walked the earth, and yet we know very little about them. To help find food, they use sophisticated teamwork and ingenious hunting techniques that have rarely been witnessed.
Although the open ocean seems like a featureless expanse, it is shaped by powerful currents that flow across the globe like invisible rivers. These currents transport animals, nutrients and entire ecosystems across immense distances. For ocean drifters such as Smith's swimming crabs, the currents are both a lifeline and a gamble, carrying them through a world where danger can appear without warning.
Currents also drive one of the largest floating ecosystems on the planet. Today, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt stretches over 5,000 miles across the ocean. But changing conditions are sweeping unprecedented amounts of this seaweed onto coastlines throughout the Caribbean. On the beaches of Mexico, turtle hatchlings emerging from their nests face a daunting new obstacle as mountains of sargassum block their path to the sea. Their struggle reveals how changes in the open ocean can have profound consequences far beyond the horizon.
In the Pacific, we follow one of nature's greatest aerial pirates, a frigatebird mother raising her chick alone.

programme.title: Blue Planet III
programme.desc:
The oceans have seasons just as the land does. Stretching across the temperate bands located between the freezing poles and the warm tropics lie the seasonal seas. Life is tough in these constantly changing waters, but if animals can persevere and adapt to change, there are myriad opportunities to not only survive but thrive here.
Winter in the seasonal seas is a battlefield. Storms whip up immense waves that can travel for thousands of miles, building to 30 metres in height before making landfall. On the Pacific coast of South America, such waves impact the lives of South America sea lions that have lived on this exposed coast for generations. Newborn pups and mothers are restricted to the colony, but the most intrepid males take a risk, leaving the tempestuous coast for unfamiliar waters and unusual prey - black-necked swans.
Some choose to escape, whilst others are undeterred by winters icy grip on the seasonal seas. In Patagonia, a female southern right whale arrives in the protected bay where she was likely born, in search of a mate. Testing prospective partners before accepting the best mate, she is rewarded with a gentle belly rub and embrace - a valuable pairing given that these animals were hunted to near extinction in the last century. The whaling ban increased this population from just 300 to 25,000, with a surprising twist – white calves.
As daylight lengthens and spring approaches, the greening of the seasonal seas commences. Plankton multiplies, creating huge blooms and feeding many species, including a rather peculiar crustacean, a porcelain crab. In the waters off Chile, over 200 million feast on this bounty, forming the largest-known aggregation of crabs in our oceans. But with limited space and an increased flow of plankton, the crabs do something remarkable - they organise themselves into structured lines, a behaviour that has never been filmed before.
As forests flourish on land, they also do so in the water. In spring, kelp, one of the fastest-growing organisms on earth, can lengthen by half a metre a day, forming submarine jungles that are home to a variety of creatures. In Japan, these lush fronds conceal a rarely seen fish, an eelpout, with a length of just ten centimetres.

In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Will and Dom are in Aberfeldy’s Crannog Centre, where visitors experience recreations of 5,000-year-old traditional dwellings. After a devastating fire three years ago put the project in jeopardy, thatcher Scott is looking to the future and building a new cookhouse, using traditional techniques and local materials. It could mean big business for the centre and increased opportunities to work with the local community, but creating Iron Age dwellings in the modern age is anything but simple.
Will then heads off to Scone Palace, crowning place of Scottish kings, to meet a couple with a family heirloom in need of rescue. It’s a handwritten Gaelic piping music book, handed down from Ian’s great-grandfather Donald, known as the Hero of Alma after his actions in the Crimean War. Now severely damaged, the music in its brittle pages might be lost forever if bookbinder Chris Shaw cannot bring it back from the brink. Ian will never play the songs it contains, as he has been battling motor neurone disease for the past decade, but he hopes if Chris Shaw is successful, the book can be passed down to his own son, also named Donald in honour of his ancestor.
Always in search of a new challenge, Dom joins a Perth-based family business whose handmade sporrans are the perfect accessory to Scotland’s famous kilts. It’s a critically endangered heritage craft that dates back to the 12th century, and the family is turning to technology to keep up with the challenge faced by cheaper, mass-produced versions made abroad. Dom is always eager to get on the tools, so what will his hosts make of his attempts at leatherworking? programme.title: Young, British and Tradwife
programme.desc:
Tradwives are trending. The term is in the dictionary, and the hashtag has over 300 million views on TikTok. Online tradwives promote the pleasures of domesticity and teach others how to be perfect homemakers in effortless and elegant social media videos that generate millions of likes. But they are not just an online phenomenon. Women in the real world, inspired by online influencers, are increasingly rejecting feminism, workplace hustle and hook-up culture to bake sourdough, homeschool the kids and obey their husbands.
BAFTA- and Grierson Award-nominated documentarian Poppy Jay wants to know why the tradwife world of domestic chores and submission appeals to so many. Reflecting on her own experience of forced marriage, she packs away her camera, pins on an apron and meets with British tradwives to find out if this is what true choice looks like in the 21st century.
As she juggles baking, sewing and schooling, she asks if a movement that demands submission to a husband is the solution to modern burnout or just the latest manifestation of an age-old misogynistic culture shaped by men, for men.
Poppy meets women from across the tradwife spectrum, from the newly married coach of ‘biblical wifery’ with 70,000 TikTok followers to the homeschooling mother of seven, to discover why the simple life rooted in traditional Christian values is suddenly so popular. Immersing herself in family life, Poppy challenges her own preconceptions, asking why any women would choose to submit to her husband and whether feminism has, as the tradwives claim, betrayed women by promising them they can have it all. programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Ayrshire - Restoring Robert Burns Graffiti ║ S1
programme.desc:
Carpenter Will and horologist Steve are far from home today, exploring Ayrshire on Scotland’s west coast. Their first stop is the Scottish Boat Building School in Irvine, where Tom is waiting with a very unusual vessel. It’s a three-piece canoe designed in the 1930s and small enough to fit in the guard’s van of a train, which meant tourists could bring their own canoes on holiday in the years before owning a car was commonplace. It represents a different kind of freedom for Tom, though. His achondroplasia means a regular-size canoe is too difficult to manoeuvre. If this folding version can be fixed, he will finally have the freedom to take his daughter out exploring the waterways of Britain.
Ayrshire is the birthplace of Scotland’s national poet, Robert Burns, and many of the towns and villages in the region can boast strong links to his life and works. So it’s no surprise that when Will is called to Barr Castle in Galston, he comes face-to-face with a very special artefact. It’s a windowpane with a hand inscription by Robert Burns himself. However, it has suffered some damage in the past, so for decades its current custodians have had it hidden away in a cupboard for safekeeping. With the help of ceramics expert Kirsten Ramsay, they hope to once again put it on display. Fixing glass is notoriously difficult, and Kirsten definitely feels the pressure of getting such an important object looking back to its best.
While in the area, Steve takes the chance to visit Kays in Mauchline, who have been crafting curling stones for over 170 years. Using a dense granite quarried from a single Scottish island, these dedicated craftspeople hone stones of unparalleled quality for use in the Winter Olympics. Steve gets the chance to help with the process, but will it be gold, silver or bronze for his efforts? programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
Five chefs remain in the race for a place in the quarter-final. But two more high-pressure challenges, which will test every aspect of their cooking, stand in their way.
Marcus and Monica are joined by special guest Adejoké Bakare, whose restaurant Chishuru is at the forefront of West African fine dining. In 2024, Adejoké became the first black woman in the UK to be awarded a coveted Michelin star. Now she’s setting the chefs a dish from her own repertoire: mushroom moin moin, served with a shito sauce and steamed egg.
It may sound simple, but this deceptively complex dish is packed with unfamiliar ingredients, techniques and flavours, and only one of the chefs has ever cooked moin moin before. With no recipe to follow, they’ll have to rely entirely on their palates, instincts and technical skills to recreate Adejoké’s dish. But with a place in the quarter-final on the line, get it wrong and the consequences could be huge.
Next up, it all comes down to dessert. The chefs have one last opportunity to convince Marcus and Monica that they deserve to stay in the competition.
But pastry is an unforgiving business. Every element must be precise, every second counts, and even the smallest mistake can unravel a dish. The judges want more than technical perfection… they’re looking for personality, originality, and a dessert that leaves a lasting impression. Who can hold their nerve when it matters most? programme.title: BBC New Comedy Awards
programme.desc:
The BBC’s biggest comedy talent search has reached its final night. Almost 1,000 comedians applied to this year’s New Comedy Awards. More than 100 went head-to-head at showcases across the country, and just 30 made it through to the knockout heats. Now only six remain.
The finalists take to the stage one last time, each hoping to win over the judges and be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026.
The grand final is filmed in front of a full house at Birmingham’s iconic Town Hall. Presenting the night is award-winning writer, comedian and Hollywood actor Guz Khan, who made the journey from stand-up to the screen and knows exactly what the night means to the acts waiting in the wings.
Leading the judging panel is the multitalented and multi-award-winning comedian, actor and writer Amy Gledhill. Joining her are Kiell Smith-Bynoe, star of Ghosts and Taskmaster, and Dan Tiernan, a former BBC New Comedy Awards winner. Together, they weigh up the writing, the delivery and the originality of every act before choosing their winner.
Rounding off the night is a very special performance from last year’s winner, Eli Hart, who returns to hand over the award to this year’s champion.
The winner will receive a paid commission to write and perform their own 30-minute audio pilot under the mentorship of a BBC comedy commissioner, plus a trophy and £1,000 in cash. For a comic at the start of their career, it is a rare opportunity that could open plenty of doors.
Now in their 30th year, the New Comedy Awards have helped launch the careers of comedy greats who regularly feature on our stages and screens, including Peter Kay, Lee Mack, Russell Howard, Romesh Ranganathan, Alan Carr, Sarah Millican, Josie Long and Joe Lycett.
The finalists are hoping to follow in their footsteps.
Six comics. One stage. One title. Who will be crowned BBC New Comedian 2026? programme.title: The Repair Shop on the Road
programme.sub-title: Highlands - Treasure in the Attic ║ S1
programme.desc:
In this episode, the experts lend their skills to a community project, hear the story behind a new treasure to be repaired and visit a local crafting hero.
Joining Dom in the Highlands is Inverness-born traditional building conserver Rich. They are on the way to Nairn Museum, where renovations have revealed some unusual wall decorations – artworks painted directly on the bare walls of the museum's attic. Left behind by Polish soldiers stationed there during World War II, this art will be lost forever if it can’t be removed. However, removing century-old plaster is a delicate business, so there is no guarantee the artworks will survive the process.
Dom then travels to North Kessock to collect another precious item to be repaired back at the barn. He meets Carole, whose unusual clockwork ship in a glass dome evokes happy memories of childhood holidays in the Wester Ross village of Plockton. However, the paper sea it once sailed on is brittle and torn, and the tune no longer plays. Will David Burville be able to get this family heirloom - handed down from Carole’s great-aunt Elsie - making music on the high seas again?
While Dom and Rich have their hands full at the museum, Will is in Beauly to meet Alan MacPherson, who has gone from keen shinty player to shinty stick maker. Now producing more than 1,400 shinty sticks each year from his Highland workshop, Alan instructs Will in the intricacies of creating equipment to stand up to the rigors of this hard-fought game. Once the woodwork is over, it is time for Will to test his sporting prowess. programme.title: MasterChef: The Professionals
programme.desc:
The four chefs who have survived the intensity of the heats are back in the kitchen. Now they must prove to Marcus and Monica that they have the consistency, confidence and creativity to take on the next level of the competition.
First up is the invention test, where the chefs must put pistachio centre stage and show Marcus and Monica what they can do with it. It’s an ingredient that naturally lends itself to pastry and desserts, but used cleverly in a savoury dish, it could give one chef the edge. Will anyone dare to take it somewhere unexpected?
But the chefs aren’t finished yet. Their next test takes them out of the kitchen and into the company of three of the country’s most influential food critics: William Sitwell, Jimi Famurewa and, taking her place alongside them for the first time, Ixta Belfrage, a recipe developer and cookbook author who spent five years working at the Ottolenghi Test Kitchen.
The chefs must cook a two-course menu that showcases their food, ideas and technical ability, knowing that every element will be scrutinised by some of the toughest palates in the business. This is their chance to prove they can produce food that excites and surprises. However, impressing three professional critics is no easy feat, and their verdicts could have a major bearing on what happens next.
Back in the kitchen, Marcus and Monica must weigh up everything they have seen and tasted before deciding which chefs have done enough to progress. With only three places in knockout week available, one mistake, an underwhelming plate or a missed opportunity could make all the difference. Who will earn their place in the next stage – and whose journey ends here?
The pressure is mounting as the chefs edge closer to the coveted MasterChef: The Professionals title. Judge - Marcus Wareing Judge - Monica Galetti Series Editor - Antonia Lloyd Series Director - Emma Reynolds Executive Producer - Kelly Sparks Production Company - Shine TV.

What begins as a side project soon intersects directly with Rose’s murder case, revealing a shocking connection between the spiked cigarettes circulating among the youth and Andrew's unpleasant death.
Joining forces once again, Rose and Joe must navigate a muddle of illicit drug dealing, cut-throat commercial feuds, a shady ashes scandal and a volatile love triangle. Together, they traverse the Northumberland coast to piece together the truth and catch a killer before anyone else gets hurt, or worse...
